To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the GKA Piragliatin repairs diverse defects of β‐cell function in human and murine islets, including those of T2DM, GK mutations and acute sulphonyurea treatment.

the pharmacological activation of glucokinase (the glucose sensor of β‐cells) reverses the defects in glucose‐induced secretion of insulin in islets from patients with type 2 Diabetes, from mice carrying mutations that mimic Maturity Onset of Diabetes of the Young and Permanent Neonatal Diabetic Mellitus linked to glucokinase mutations and in islets treated in tissue culture with sulphonylureas.

acute pharmacological glucokinases activation (Piragliatine) reverses the defects of insulin secretion and glucose‐stimulated calcium responses of β‐cells from humans with type‐2 diabetes mellitus, mice with GK mutations and mice β‐cells rendered glucose insensitive by glyburide treatment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular basis of the regulation of glucose‐induced secretion from the pancreatic β‐cell.
understanding the molecular mechanisms of the action of GKAs and the therapeutic potential of this strategy in diabetes mellitus.

the molecular basis of the regulation of insulin secretion in health and diabetes and the molecular pathogenesis of the disease, with particular emphasis on the role of the glucose sensor, glucokinase, as well as the molecular basis of sulphonylureas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
pharmacological GK activation is an effective and safe way to restore the function of β‐cells and thus represents a promising new strategy to improve the management of T2DM.
the results of this study support the concept of GKAs as a novel class of antidiabetic drugs.
the GKA‐Piragliatin is an effective agent in restoring the defective glucose‐induced secretion in diverse forms of β‐cell failure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GKAs have a potential for the treatment of diverse defects in β‐cells, including the multifactorial defects in T2DM.
pharmacological activation of glucose metabolism in β‐cells by a GKA is a promising strategy for the treatment of diabetes mellitus.
the GKA Piragliatin is able to reverse the defects in β‐cell function of islets from humans and mice, and thus may be useful in the treatment of diabetes mellitus in both species.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GKAs are a viable strategy for the development of new antidiabetic drugs.

the GKA approach is a viable one for the repair of diverse diabetic β‐cell defects and that it should be pursued in a concerted manner with the goal of developing a safe and effective drug for clinical use in diabetes.

GKAs have potential to be developed into effective antidiabetic drugs, but the clinical trials need to be designed in a manner that is different from that of the trials with sulphonylureas and other drugs.
